Understood what the dog was saying
She was scared, and a frightened dog can bite when it feels cornered.
Exactly. Fear signals: tail tucked, ears back, body low, looking away, lip licking.
She was relaxed. The owner knows their own dog.
A relaxed dog has a loose, wiggly body and a neutral or gently wagging tail. Pepper showed the opposite.
Learn the fear signals: tucked tail, ears back, low body, looking away.
She was inviting play. Dogs crouch when they want to play.
A play bow has the rear end UP, a loose body and a wagging tail. Pepper was low all over with her tail tucked.
A play bow (rear up, loose, wagging) looks very different from a fearful crouch.
Read the dog, not just the owner's reassurance. Ask for the dog to be secured.
It's 102°F with a heat advisory. Watch your HYDRATION and BODY HEAT meters (top right).
Standing in the sun, walking and carrying loads all heat you up. Shade, the truck's AC and water bring you back down.
In the truck, E at the back of the doorway gives you water or the AC; outside, E by the truck is water too. Rest in the shade under trees.
Learn the warning signs of heat illness, and act on them the moment they show up.
Drink water before you're thirsty: small amounts at every stop through a hot shift.
Use shade and AC to cool down between stops, and pace yourself in extreme heat.
Dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps or confusion: stop, cool down, hydrate and tell dispatch. Collapse or confusion means call 911.
Your head is pounding and the sidewalk feels like it's tilting. Your legs are heavy and you feel a little sick.
These are warning signs of heat illness. What do you do?
Responded to heat illness warning signs
Stop now. Get into the shade or the truck's AC, drink water, and tell dispatch if you don't feel better quickly.
Acting at the first signs stops heat exhaustion turning into heat stroke, which is a medical emergency.
Push through. Only a couple of stops left, then you'll rest.
Heat illness gets worse fast. "Pushing through" is how heat exhaustion becomes heat stroke.
Never push through heat illness symptoms. Stop, cool down, hydrate and get help.
Grab an energy drink and keep moving.
Caffeine and sugar don't cool you down or rehydrate you, and can make dehydration worse.
Water (or an electrolyte drink) and cooling down treat heat stress. Energy drinks don't.
You sip water slowly in the cool air until the pounding eases.
Copy that. Take the time you need. Your safety comes first. Call us straight away if it gets worse.

Three doorsteps where the people are the hard part: someone angry, someone you can't easily talk to, and someone who isn't who the package is for.
Walk with A/D, SHIFT to walk carefully, E to interact, TAB for the handheld.
Stay calm, stay polite, and keep to the delivery rules however the conversation goes.

88 Cedar St: SIGNATURE REQUIRED. The package is a day late.
Finally! This was supposed to be here YESTERDAY. I stayed home all day for it!
Do you people even look at the dates?
Calmed an upset customer
"I'm sorry you waited in all day, that's really frustrating. It's here now. If you want it on record, I'll give you the number to report the delay."
Acknowledge first, then offer something real. Most anger is about not being heard.
"Sorry about that. Can I get a signature?"
Polite, but it skips the part the customer needed: hearing that their day was wasted, and what they can do about it.
With an upset customer, acknowledge the problem before you ask for anything.
"I just deliver what they give me. It's not my fault."
It may be true, but it sounds like a brush-off and makes it worse. You are the company at the door.
Don't argue about blame at the door: acknowledge, apologize for the experience, and offer the next step.
…Okay. Thank you. Where do I sign?
Unbelievable. Just give it here.
Acknowledge the problem, apologize for the experience, offer the next step. Then the signature.
14 Alder Ln: SIGNATURE REQUIRED.
¡Hola! ¿Es un paquete para mí?
The customer asks, in Spanish, whether the package is theirs, and doesn't seem to speak much English.
You need a signature. What do you do?
Got a signature across a language barrier
Smile, show the label and point to the name on it, then turn the handheld round to the signature box: "¿Firma, por favor?"
The label, pointing and the screen do the talking. A couple of words of the customer's language are a kindness, not a requirement.
Say "Sign here" slowly and point at the screen.
That works. Showing their own name on the label first tells them it really is theirs.
Say it again, louder, in English.
Louder isn't clearer, and it feels like shouting. Show, don't repeat.
Across a language barrier: the label, pointing and the handheld screen. Not volume.
Leave the package on the step and go.

A signature-required package is never left unattended, however awkward the conversation.
¿Perdón? No entiendo…

¡Ah, sí! Ana Morales. ¡Gracias!
Show the label and the signature screen. A smile and a few words go further than volume.
22 Birch Ln: SIGNATURE REQUIRED for Priya Nair.
Nobody home and a signature needed: record the exception on your handheld (TAB) and leave a door tag.
A man walks up the drive behind you.

Kept a signature package from someone who isn't the customer
"Thanks, that's kind. But this one needs Priya's own signature, so I can't leave it with anyone else. I'll leave her a notice."
Polite and firm. The rule protects Priya, and a friendly stranger is exactly who it protects her from.
"Can you show me some ID first?"

A signature-required package goes to the recipient (or someone they arranged), not to whoever offers.
"Great, sign here and it's yours."

You think better of it before he can sign: the package stays with you. On a real route, that would have been too late.
Alright, no worries.
Nobody home + signature required = exception, a door tag, and the package stays with you. Whoever offers to take it.
A good load is a fast, safe route. A bad one is an hour of digging and a sore back.

Drag each package from the cart onto the shelves (or arrow keys to choose, ENTER to pick up and put down). Hover a package to read its full label. Sections are by stop: A = stops 1-3 (nearest the door), B = 4-6, C = 7-9.
Heavy (35 lb+) goes low — bottom shelf or floor. Nothing heavy above shoulder height.
Fragile stays off the floor, the floor bays are for heavy or bulky freight, and dangerous goods go in the marked zone. Once everything is in, strap the floor load (T), then roll out (R).
Load in reverse stop order so the first stops are nearest the door: less digging at every stop.
Heavy low, light high. Weight above shoulder height is how backs and heads get hurt.
Strap or brace the floor load. Loose freight shifts the first time you brake hard.

Notice how much time the misloads cost. That's why loading matters.
Check number AND street AND unit before you pull a package.
